items.prompt: What actually stops ApplicationCore's domain code from depending on EF Core or ASP.NET?
items.answer: Its project file has no reference to EF Core or ASP.NET
distractors: A code review rule that the team enforces on every PR
Its repository interfaces are all marked internal
A Roslyn analyzer that fails the build on EF usings
items.explanation: The core owns contracts like IRepository and IEmailSender; Infrastructure implements them. Failure modes: entities importing DbContext, services returning IActionResult, leaking IQueryable.

items.prompt: Why can a service get an IRepository<Basket> but not an IRepository<BasketItem>?
items.answer: EfRepository<T> requires T to implement IAggregateRoot, which BasketItem does not
distractors: BasketItem has no DbSet of its own, so EF cannot build a repository for it
BasketItem is a value object without an Id, so it cannot be loaded by key
Repositories are registered by hand, and only Basket and Order were registered
items.explanation: The constraint stops you loading a BasketItem independently of its Basket - the repository enforces aggregate boundaries.

items.prompt: OrderWithItemsByIdSpec filters only by order Id and includes the items. What is wrong with it?
items.answer: It never filters by buyer, so any user can load any order by id
distractors: It over-fetches the whole catalog graph through ThenInclude
It has no paging, so large orders make the query time out
It cannot be reused, because the order id is hard-coded inside it
items.explanation: The pattern catalog's failure mode for Specification: a spec missing a security filter - the drill asks you to write the missing predicate.

items.prompt: Adding a catalog item that is already in the basket calls Basket.AddItem. What happens, and why is that rule safe?
items.answer: The existing line's quantity grows; only AddItem can change the private item list
distractors: A second line is added, and the UI merges duplicate lines when displaying the basket
BasketService checks for a duplicate line before it calls the repository's update
EF's unique index on CatalogItemId rejects the duplicate line when the basket saves
items.explanation: The aggregate root owns a private collection and exposes a read-only view; callers cannot mutate Items directly.

items.prompt: OrderItem embeds CatalogItemOrdered (name, picture) as an owned type instead of just a foreign key to the catalog item. Why?
items.answer: To preserve what was bought even if the catalog item later changes
distractors: Owned types are faster to query than a join in SQL Server
EF cannot map a foreign key from OrderItems to the Catalog table
So that past orders can be edited by changing the catalog item
items.explanation: It is denormalisation for history, mapped as an owned type embedded in OrderItems.

items.prompt: CatalogItem uses HiLo id generation. What does that buy?
items.answer: Client-side ids from reserved blocks, so inserts can batch
distractors: Globally unique GUID ids that work across databases
Reuse of ids freed by deleted rows in the table
Ids that are hidden from public API consumers
items.explanation: HiLo reserves a range of ids from a sequence; EF assigns them before the insert.

items.prompt: Checkout calls CreateOrderAsync, then DeleteBasketAsync - each with its own SaveChanges and no explicit transaction. What can a crash between them leave?
items.answer: An order that was created while its basket still lingers
distractors: A deleted basket with no order
Nothing, because EF wraps consecutive SaveChanges calls in one transaction
A half-written order with some items missing
items.explanation: Within one SaveChanges EF uses an implicit transaction; across calls there is no atomicity unless you open one. On the money path that gap is worth calling out.

items.prompt: The FixShipToAddress migration makes the owned Address columns NOT NULL with defaultValue: "". What would happen without the default on a table with existing null values?
items.answer: The NOT NULL change would fail on rows that still hold nulls
distractors: EF would silently delete the rows that still hold nulls
It would succeed and the existing nulls would stay as nulls
The migration's Down method would run automatically instead
items.explanation: Migration authors must handle existing rows; this one also has a real Down, making it reversible.

items.prompt: How does the Web app add catalog caching without touching CatalogViewModelService or its callers?
items.answer: A cached wrapper implements the same interface and DI registers it in place of the real service
distractors: CatalogViewModelService inherits from a caching base class added for the purpose
ASP.NET response-caching middleware wraps every catalog page in the Web project
EF Core's second-level cache is switched on for the catalog tables in the context
items.explanation: Decorator plus DI: callers never know caching exists; removing it is one DI line. Failure modes include caches with no invalidation.

items.prompt: Which DI lifetime mistake does the pattern catalog call the classic composition-root bug?
items.answer: A singleton capturing a scoped DbContext (a captive dependency)
distractors: Registering every repository as transient instead of scoped
Open-generic registration of IRepository<> in one line
Constructor injection instead of resolving from a service locator
items.explanation: The other options are fine or even recommended; the singleton that outlives the request keeps one DbContext alive across requests and threads.

items.prompt: Why does the PublicApi return CatalogItemDto rather than the CatalogItem entity?
distractors: System.Text.Json cannot serialise EF entities
Minimal API binding only works with DTO types
AutoMapper refuses to map from entity types
items.explanation: The mapping profile renames CatalogBrand.Brand to dto.Name without touching the entity.

items.prompt: Why put Guard.Against checks inside CatalogItem rather than only in the controller?
items.answer: So an invalid CatalogItem can never exist, whoever constructs it
distractors: Because minimal API endpoints are not allowed to throw exceptions
So the UI receives friendlier, localised validation messages
Because guard clauses placed in the domain run at compile time
items.explanation: Guard clauses enforce invariants at the entity boundary; they are distinct from user-facing model validation.

items.prompt: With one class per endpoint (REPR), what failure mode does the catalog warn about for a newly added write endpoint?
items.answer: Nothing forces it to declare the ADMINISTRATORS requirement
distractors: It cannot share request DTOs with the other endpoints
It gets registered twice, by AddEndpoints and MapEndpoints
It loses access to dependency injection for its handler
items.explanation: Cohesion and discoverability come with no enforced base behavior; the drill asks you to confirm every write endpoint requires the role.

items.front: eShopOnWeb's safe schema-change playbook: list the steps after editing the entity and its configuration.
items.back: Add the migration naming the context (-c CatalogContext, there are two); read the generated Up/Down and how existing rows are handled; add a default or backfill for non-null columns on populated tables; test on a copy with real-shaped data (not in-memory); have a rollback plan - is Down correct or one-way?

items.front: Why does eShopOnWeb have two DbContexts, and what does that mean for migrations?
items.back: CatalogContext holds domain data and AppIdentityDbContext holds ASP.NET Identity data - a deliberate boundary. Each has its own migrations history, so every dotnet ef command must name the context.

items.front: Rank schema changes by blast radius, and what does a senior ask that a junior skips?
items.back: Adding a nullable column is low risk (additive); making a column non-null, renaming or dropping is high risk. A senior reads the SQL, asks what happens to the existing rows, checks nullability/defaults/locking, plans deploy order (migrate before or after code) and confirms Down works.

items.front: What does MediatR (CQRS-lite handlers) buy eShopOnWeb, and what does it cost?
items.back: Thin controllers and small, isolated, unit-testable handlers - at the cost of indirection and jump-to-definition friction; overuse adds an indirection tax and fat handlers become the old service in disguise.
